If so, how did it go? I'm thinking about doing it, but I have questions. Many questions.
Has anyone in /v/AskElectronics ever built their own CNC router from a kit?

Yes! I built a Shapeoko 2 kit a couple years ago. What would you like to know?

Everything was very straightforward (with that kit anyway). There were two hard bits: one was tapping the rails to screw the frame together (which was only hard because tapping things in general is hard), and the other was the wiring / cable management, which I ended up redoing. The wiring itself was simple but keeping the sheaf of wires from getting caught on anything required a lot of zip ties and general annoyance.

I have a tone of questions. Seriously. I'm thinking of building one for my sign shop. I'd need to build the biggest one they make. Industrial machines similar to what I need cost $10k-$30k which I cannot afford.

How durable are they? - I'm looking to be able to route 1/4in acryllic sheets and .080 aluminum to make sign letters. The big machines tear through that stuff like butter.

What software do you use? Would I be able to take an EPS file and route shapes?

Do you need to build a separate vacuum table for it? Industrial machines have one to keep the material on the cut pad and prevent your cutouts from being chucked across the room. In

In your opinion, would it work well in a light industrial setting? For example, routing a set of letters from acrylic once a week.

Are the parts easy to replace if something breaks?

I'm sure I have more questions, but I don't want to be greedy.

Size: mine's not that big, 24x24 I think, but you can make them as big as the rails you put on them (the Shapeoko anyway). Especially if you don't need super accuracy on the z axis: I use mine to make circuit boards so it's dialed in perfectly near the center, but I'm doing depths of like 0.2mm.

Durability: acrylic is fine. I use 1/8" acrylic all the time and I can cut through it no problem. The things to watch out for are, if you use a different kind of plastic then it'll tend to melt instead of cut, but acrylic works great. If you have problems getting it to cut smoothly you can always lower the feed rate, too.

Software: I use CamBam. It doesn't import EPS but it will do DXF. I'm sure you can find a utility that will convert EPS to something CamBam will read, or there are plenty of other options for software. The way it works is, you get one thing that you run on your desktop that lets you draw things and set tool parameters and such, and that writes out a GCode file. Then, the machine has a computer driving it that reads GCode and sends it to the controller, which turns the motors and cuts things.

Vacuum table: I just drilled a bunch of holes in the waste board and use wooden clamps to hold stuff down. A vacuum table would work too but it seems like overkill. I will say, tape isn't anywhere near strong enough, you'll want some kind of clamp or something.

Routing letters once a week seems perfect. I use mine for stuff like that, I make cases for electronic stuff out of acrylic. If you pick up a strip heater also, you'd be amazed what you can build by routing a shape out of an acrylic sheet and then folding it up.

Parts: if it's a kit, absolutely. You're going to need to replace the bit every so often, it'll dull, and I had a power supply bite the dust. For the Shapeoko, the only things that are specific to the kit and not just standard hardware are the end plates that the rails / carriage screw on to, everything else can be ordered from McMaster-Carr. And I don't even know how you'd manage to break those.

This is very cool. What do you mean by "routing a shape out of an acrylic sheet and then folding it up?"

What do you do with these creations? How do you come up with what to build? Is it for school, or work? Does owning the CNC pay for itself?

/greed

Here's a picture, maybe it'll be clearer: http://i.imgur.com/hVWGiNu.jpg

Imagine a papercraft thing: cut out a shape, fold along some lines, and now it's a 3d object. What I do is, I cut that shape out of 1/8" acrylic, "score" it by cutting 1/16" deep along lines I want to fold, then put it over a strip heater. A strip heater is a heating element shaped like a long line, that you can lay a sheet of acrylic over until it heats up and gets floppy, then you can bend it and when it cools it will hold the new shape. So with that, I can fold my cut-out-acrylic-sheet into whatever I want. You'd be surprised at the stuff you can make that way.

As far as what I do with them, nothing really. I just make stuff for myself. I've got a 3d printer too, I've taken a few jobs for money with that, earned like maybe $100 total, but I wasn't trying to advertise a lot or anything. Mostly I just do this as a hobby. I like making things. :)
